_metadata.program: Bachelor of Technology (B.Tech) in Computer Science and Engineering

courses.title: Introduction to Programming
courses.objectives: Basics of programming using C; Basic UNIX commands, Primitives and Datatypes, Arithmetic operations, Input and output functions; Conditional statement; Loops, Introduction to Functions, Macros, Recursion, Arrays, Strings, Dynamic Memory Allocation, Pointers, Complex Data Types, File Handling, Introduction to Linked List, sorting, Searching, Bitwise Operator.

courses.title: Mathematics-I
courses.objectives: Differential and Integral Calculus: Rolle's theorem, Mean value theorems, Taylor's and Maclaurin theorems, Maxima and minima, Indeterminate forms; Linear Algebra: Matrices, Systems of linear equations, Gauss elimination, Vector spaces, Subspaces, Linear independence, Basis and dimension, Linear transformations, Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, Diagonalization, Cayley-Hamilton Theorem.

courses.title: Physics for Engineers
courses.objectives: Classical Mechanics, Oscillations and Waves: Simple harmonic motion, Damped and driven oscillators, Resonance; Quantum Mechanics: Wave-particle duality, De Broglie hypothesis, Heisenberg uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation, Particle in a box; Optics and Lasers: Interference, Diffraction, Polarization, Principles of Lasers and optical fibers.

courses.title: Applied Chemistry
courses.objectives: Molecular structure and spectroscopy; Thermodynamics and chemical kinetics; Electrochemistry and corrosion; Polymer chemistry and smart materials; Nanomaterials and green chemistry principles for modern engineering applications.

courses.title: Digital Fabrication
courses.objectives: Introduction to Computer-Aided Design (CAD), 3D printing technologies (FDM, SLA), CNC machining, laser cutting, PCB prototyping, rapid tooling, and integration of mechanical fabrication with digital electronics.

courses.title: Basic Electrical Engineering
courses.objectives: DC Circuit analysis, Thevenin and Norton theorems, Maximum power transfer theorem; AC circuits, Phasors, Single-phase and three-phase circuits, Power and power factor; Magnetic circuits and Transformers; DC machines and Induction motors.

courses.title: Basic Electronics Engineering
courses.objectives: Semiconductor physics, p-n junction diodes, Zener diodes, diode circuits and rectifiers; Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJTs) and Field Effect Transistors (FETs, MOSFETs); Operational Amplifiers (Op-Amps) and linear/non-linear applications; Digital logic basics, logic gates, truth tables, and boolean minimization.

courses.title: Mathematics-II
courses.objectives: Multivariable Calculus: Functions of several variables, partial derivatives, directional derivatives, gradient, curl, divergence, line, surface, and volume integrals, Green's, Stokes', and Gauss divergence theorems; Ordinary Differential Equations: First-order ODEs, higher-order linear ODEs with constant coefficients, series solutions, Laplace transforms.

courses.title: Probability & Statistics
courses.objectives: Probability theory: Axioms of probability, Conditional probability, Bayes' theorem; Random variables and distributions (discrete and continuous): Binomial, Poisson, Geometric, Uniform, Exponential, Normal; Joint distributions, covariance, correlation; Sampling distributions, Central Limit Theorem; Estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, regression analysis.

courses.title: Discrete Mathematics
courses.objectives: Sets, relations, functions, Equivalence and Partial order relations; Formal logic: Propositional logic and truth tables, normal forms, Predicates and Quantification; Notion of proof: proof techniques, Mathematical Induction; Combinatorics: Basic counting techniques, The pigeonhole principle, countable and uncountable sets, recurrence relations, The principle of Inclusion-exclusion; Graph theory: Graph terminology, representation of graphs, Isomorphism, trees, Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs, Graph coloring and Planar graphs; Number theory: Divisibility, GCD, The Euclidean algorithm, The fundamental theorem of arithmetic, Modular arithmetic; Group theory: Groups, subgroups, finite groups, cyclic groups, permutation groups.

courses.title: Data Structures
courses.objectives: Stacks, Queues, Lists; Sorting and Searching; Trees, Tree Traversals; Heaps, Priority Queues; Binary Search, Binary Search Trees, Balanced BSTs (AVL, Red-Black Trees); Hashing and Hash Tables; Graphs: Representations, Depth First Search, Breadth First Search, Topological Sort.

courses.title: Software Tools & Technologies Lab
courses.objectives: Basics of Linux: Linux commands, shell scripting, text editors (Vim/Emacs); Scripting languages (Python/Bash); Web programming (HTML, CSS, JS, REST APIs); Plotting tools (Gnuplot, Matplotlib); Document processing tools (LaTeX, Markdown); Version control systems (Git, GitHub workflows); Debuggers (gdb, valgrind); Containerization with Docker.

courses.title: Computer Organization and Architecture
courses.objectives: Introduction: Overview of basic digital building blocks, truth tables, basic structure of a digital computer, number representation; Machine Instructions and Program: Assembly language programming for processors; Arithmetic Unit: Basic building blocks for the ALU, adder, subtractor, shifter, multiplication and division circuits, control path microprogramming, hardwired control; Memory organization: ROM, RAM, EPROM, Flash, cache memories, cache coherence protocol for uniprocessor, virtual memory, secondary storage; Input/Output Organization: I/O subblock, interrupts, polling, DMA; Pipelining: Instruction pipeline, hazards and forwarding.

courses.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
courses.objectives: Algorithm analysis: worst and average case, asymptotic notation, recurrences; Sorting and selection: randomized quicksort, median finding; Randomized techniques; Divide and Conquer; Dynamic programming and Greedy algorithms; Graph algorithms: BFS, DFS, Minimum Spanning Trees (Prim, Kruskal), Shortest paths (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall), Network Flow (Ford-Fulkerson); NP-Completeness, reductions, and introduction to Approximation Algorithms.

courses.title: Theory of Computation
courses.objectives: Alphabets, languages, finite automata (DFA, NFA, regular expressions, pumping lemma for regular languages); Context-Free Grammars and Context-Free Languages, parse trees, pushdown automata, CYK algorithm, pumping lemma for CFLs; Turing machines, Church-Turing thesis, decidability, halting problem, reductions; Introduction to space and time complexity, P vs NP, NP-completeness.

courses.title: Operating Systems
courses.objectives: Introduction: Virtualization, Concurrency, Persistence; CPU Virtualization: Process, Process API, PCB, mechanism, CPU scheduling, Multilevel Feedback Queue; Memory Virtualization: Address space, memory API, address translation, segmentation, paging, TLBs, replacement policies, swapping; Concurrency: Threads, thread API, locks, condition variables, semaphores, concurrency bugs; Persistence: I/O devices, Hard disks, RAID, file and directories, file system implementation; Security: OS security, authentication, access control; Practical tools and kernel hacking with xv6.

courses.title: Compiler Design
courses.objectives: Compiler structure: Analysis-synthesis model of compilation, phases of a compiler, tool-based approach to compiler construction; Phases of compiler design: Lexical analysis (Lex/Flex); Syntax analysis (LL, LR, LALR parsing, Yacc/Bison); Syntax-directed translation; Type checking and semantic analysis; Run-time system and memory layout; Intermediate code generation (Three-address code, SSA); Machine-independent optimizations (dead code elimination, loop optimizations); Target code generation and register allocation.

courses.title: Database Management Systems
courses.objectives: Database System Concepts: Data models, schemas and instances, database languages, relational DBMS architecture; Relational Algebra: Select, Project, Set operations, Join, Division; ER and EER Models: Entities, relationships, keys, specialization/generalization, schema mapping; Normalization: Functional dependencies, 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, multivalued dependencies and 4NF; Transaction Management: ACID properties, serializability, concurrency control (2PL, timestamp ordering), recovery systems (WAL, checkpoints); Indexing: B+ Trees, hashing; SQL programming and database application development.

courses.title: Artificial Intelligence
courses.objectives: Introduction and Agent Architectures; Problem Solving by Search: Uninformed search (BFS, DFS), Informed search (A*, IDA*), Heuristics, Adversarial search (Minimax, Alpha-Beta pruning), Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP); Automated Reasoning: Propositional and First-Order Logic, inference, resolution refutation, knowledge-based systems; Planning: Classical planning, STRIPS, state-space and plan-space planning; Reasoning under Uncertainty: Probabilistic reasoning, Bayesian networks, inference; Reinforcement Learning: Markov Decision Processes (MDP), Bellman equations, Value/Policy iteration, Q-learning.

courses.title: Computer Networks
courses.objectives: Introduction: Layered architecture (OSI, TCP/IP), packet switching vs circuit switching, delay, loss, and throughput; Application Layer: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, P2P, CDNs; Transport Layer: TCP, UDP, reliable data transfer, flow control, congestion control (TCP Reno, Cubic, BBR), socket programming; Network Layer: IP addressing, subnetting, CIDR, NAT, routing algorithms (Dijkstra, Distance Vector), BGP, OSPF, ICMP, IPv6; Data Link Layer: Framing, error detection/correction, MAC protocols (CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA), Ethernet, Wi-Fi; Network Security: TLS/SSL, IPSec, firewalls; Simulation tools: Wireshark, NS-3, Mininet.

courses.title: AI-Augmented Software Development
courses.objectives: Introduction to LLM-based software engineering: Role of LLMs in SDLC, coding assistants, testing and debugging support, documentation, academic integrity; Prompting as interface design: Role and task specification, constraints, structured prompting, prompt refinement; LLMs as software components: LLM APIs, request/response patterns, context handling, schema validation; From assistants to agents: Perceive-think-act-observe loops, tool use, single-agent task execution, tool registries; Agent harness engineering: Harness definition, bounded execution, step limits, runtime policies, trace logging, human-in-the-loop approvals; Evaluation harnesses: Task suites, success criteria, regression testing, step count and latency metrics; Safety and governance: Prompt injection, unsafe tool use, sandboxing, human review; Capstone team project.

courses.title: Nand to Tetris
courses.objectives: Building a modern computer from first principles: Boolean logic, logic gates, ALU design; Sequential logic, flip-flops, memory units; Machine language, Hack computer architecture; Assembly language and Hack assembler implementation; Virtual machine abstraction, stack arithmetic, memory segments, VM translator; High-level object-based language (Jack); Jack compiler (syntax analysis, code generation); Mini-operating system implementation.

courses.title: Cryptography
courses.objectives: Introduction, Formal Notions, Mathematics Recap, Historical Ciphers; Attack Models, Informational and Computational Security, Perfect Secrecy; Symmetric Key Cryptography: Stream ciphers (LFSR), Block ciphers (DES, AES), Modes of operation; Cryptanalysis: Linear and Differential Cryptanalysis; Hash Functions: SHA-2, SHA-3, HMAC, collisions, Birthday paradox; Public Key Cryptography: RSA, Diffie-Hellman, Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC); Digital Signatures and PKI; Quantum Cryptography overview.

courses.title: Approximation Algorithms
courses.objectives: Introduction to NP-completeness and approximation algorithms; Combinatorial algorithms: Greedy algorithms (Set Cover), Local search (Facility Location); Rounding data and Dynamic Programming (Knapsack FPTAS); Linear Programming (LP) relaxations and LP duality; Deterministic rounding and randomized rounding; Primal-dual schema (Vertex Cover, Network Design); Metric embeddings; Semidefinite Programming (Max-Cut); Hardness of approximation and PCP theorem overview.

courses.title: BTech Project-I
courses.objectives: Research and development-oriented capstone project based on problems of practical and theoretical interest under faculty supervision. Includes comprehensive literature survey, formulation of research methodology/system architecture, baseline experiments, interim evaluation, and written report.

courses.title: BTech Project-II
courses.objectives: Continuation of CSQ401: full implementation, experimental validation, comparative benchmark analysis, final software prototype or scientific paper manuscript, public defense presentation, and comprehensive thesis submission.

courses.title: MOOC-based (NPTEL): Advanced Computer Science
courses.objectives: Departmentally approved NPTEL / SWAYAM advanced 12-week course for credit transfer. Governed under IIT Bhilai MOOC Policy Section 3.2.1. Supervised and evaluated by DUGC Convener.

academic_rules.text: The normal semester load for undergraduate B.Tech students is governed by the semester-wise curriculum matrix, typically ranging between 17 and 19.5 credits per regular semester.

In general a student has to register for the nominal load as per the semester-wise program curriculum. Overload/underload can only be permitted from third semester onwards. BTech students may be allowed to register up to a maximum of 21 credits from their third semester onwards by the concerned DUGC conveners on a case-to-case basis.

Underload can only be permitted from third semester onwards. BTech students may be allowed to register for a minimum of 15 credits from their third semester onwards by the concerned DUGC conveners on a case-to-case basis.
In the eighth regular semester, BTech students may be allowed to register up to a minimum of 9 credits by the concerned DUGC conveners subject to fulfilling all pending credit requirements.

To be eligible for the award of a BTech in Computer Science and Engineering degree, a candidate must earn at least 144 course credits (comprising 40.5 Institute Core, 4 Program Linked, 52 Program Core, 22.5 Program Elective, 15 Open Elective, and 10 Liberal Arts) plus 12 Non-Graded Core units, maintaining a minimum CGPA of 4.5.

Pre-requisites shall be defined only in terms of other course code(s). A precedent course defined as a prerequisite for a course must be cleared (obtaining a passing grade; non-F grade) before the dependent course can be registered.
A student shall be allowed to opt for a maximum of 6 credits from MOOC-based portals (such as NPTEL / SWAYAM) for considering against credit transfer during their entire B.Tech undergraduate program.
A 14-week or 42-hour MOOC/NPTEL course shall be considered equivalent to a full-semester course worth 3 credits of IIT Bhilai. Prior departmental DUGC approval is mandatory before enrolling.

The respective DUGC convener acts as instructor-in-charge for any approved MOOC-based course (using course code format CSL495). The proctored grade is displayed on the semester grade sheet and counted directly towards CGPA calculation.

A student at the end of the 5th semester can apply to register for BTech Honours or Minor specialization in another discipline. Eligibility requires a cumulative CGPA of 8.0 or above, no active backlogs, and successful completion of 24 additional credits beyond the normal 144 credits.
academic_rules.applies_to: Undergraduate B.Tech students at completion of Semester 5

academic_rules.text: If SGPA falls below 4.5 in any semester, the student will be placed on academic probation with a warning letter issued by the Dean of Academic Affairs (DoAA). A student on probation is prohibited from participating in off-campus extracurricular events.
A student will normally not be allowed to register and their academic program will be automatically terminated if their Cumulative Grade Point Average (CGPA) falls below 4.0.
Students may add or drop courses using the academic registration system within 5 working days of the commencement of the regular semester, subject to approval by the DUGC convener.
academic_rules.applies_to: All registered students at the start of each semester

academic_rules.text: Course grade improvement examination can be carried out for a maximum of three courses where the student was awarded a grade of C or less and cumulative CGPA is less than or equal to 5.0, provided it does not increase normal semester load.
academic_rules.applies_to: Students with C or lower grade and CGPA <= 5.0

academic_rules.text: A student is required to maintain a minimum attendance of 75% in each registered course to be eligible to sit for the end-semester examination, unless granted medical dispensation by the Senate.

modules_lessons.title: Heuristic Search & Adversarial Games

modules_lessons.title: Probabilistic Reasoning & Reinforcement Learning

exercises.question: Given an unbalanced Binary Search Tree with n nodes, explain how AVL tree rotations maintain the O(log n) height invariant upon inserting a key that causes an imbalance factor of +2 at node P with a left child having balance factor -1.
exercises.answer_key: This corresponds to a Left-Right (LR) imbalance case. The restoration requires a double rotation: first a Left Rotation on the left child of P, converting the tree into a Left-Left (LL) case, followed immediately by a Right Rotation on node P. Both rotations update balance factors and restore strict AVL height balance in O(1) rotation time.

exercises.question: Formulate the Bellman recurrence relation for the 0/1 Knapsack Problem with capacity W and items (w_i, v_i). State the space complexity optimization technique.
exercises.answer_key: Recurrence: DP[i, w] = DP[i-1, w] if w_i > w; else max(DP[i-1, w], DP[i-1, w - w_i] + v_i), with base case DP[0, w] = 0. Space can be optimized from O(n*W) to O(W) using a single 1D array traversed backwards from W down to w_i to avoid overwriting values needed from the previous iteration.

exercises.question: Explain the four Coffman conditions necessary for a deadlock to occur. How does the Banker's algorithm prevent deadlock by denying requests that lead to unsafe states?
exercises.answer_key: The four Coffman conditions are: 1. Mutual Exclusion, 2. Hold and Wait, 3. No Preemption, 4. Circular Wait. The Banker's algorithm runs a safety check before granting any resource allocation: it simulates allocating the requested resources and verifies whether there exists at least one sequence of process completions where all remaining claims (Need matrix <= Work vector) can be satisfied without deadlock.

exercises.question: Use the Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages to demonstrate that L = {0^n 1^n | n >= 0} is not regular.
exercises.answer_key: Assume L is regular with pumping length p. Choose string s = 0^p 1^p in L (|s| = 2p >= p). According to the lemma, s = xyz with |xy| <= p and |y| >= 1. Since |xy| <= p, y consists entirely of 0s (y = 0^k, k >= 1). Pumping with i = 2 gives xy^2z = 0^(p+k) 1^p. Since k >= 1, the number of 0s exceeds the number of 1s, so xy^2z is not in L, contradicting regularity. Thus, L is not regular.

exercises.question: In TCP Reno congestion control, what triggers Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery, and how is the Congestion Window (cwnd) adjusted compared to a timeout event?
exercises.answer_key: Fast Retransmit is triggered upon receiving 3 duplicate ACKs (4 identical ACKs total), signaling that a single packet was lost while subsequent packets arrived out-of-order. Instead of dropping cwnd to 1 MSS (as in a timeout), TCP Reno sets ssthresh = cwnd / 2, sets cwnd = ssthresh + 3 MSS (Fast Recovery), retransmits the missing segment, and increments cwnd by 1 MSS for each additional duplicate ACK received until an ACK acknowledging the new data arrives.
